claims.text: Depositing a sub-monolayer amount of Pt will produce atomically dispersed single-atom Pt sites on the near-equiatomic multi-principal-element alloy surface.
The Pt addition will not significantly increase the catalyst's overall platinum-group-metal loading.
The unmodified alloy has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
The unmodified alloy contains minimal or no platinum.
The deposited single-atom Pt sites will become embedded in or stabilized by the high-entropy alloy matrix.
High configurational entropy will limit agglomeration and sintering of the Pt sites.
Isolated Pt atoms will modify the local electronic environment of the alloy surface.
The Pt-induced electronic modification will facilitate CO oxidation.
The Pt-induced electronic modification will facilitate hydrocarbon oxidation.
The Pt-induced electronic modification will facilitate NO oxidation.
The isolated Pt sites will weaken the binding of poisoning species such as H2O and NO.
Anchoring by the high-entropy matrix will prevent Pt sintering and deactivation during long-term high-temperature or hydrothermal exposure.
The Pt-modified catalyst will have a lower CO-oxidation T50 than the unmodified catalyst.
The Pt-modified catalyst will resist deactivation by H2O better than the unmodified catalyst.
The Pt-modified catalyst will resist deactivation by NO better than the unmodified catalyst.
The Pt-modified catalyst will retain performance better than the unmodified catalyst during accelerated aging.
The enhanced activity and poison resistance will apply during transient operation below 150 °C in H2O- and NO-containing simulated automotive exhaust.
The durability benefit will persist over aging conditions that simulate vehicle-lifetime degradation.
